text.p: ITT Corp. late on Thursday rejected Hilton Hotels Corp.'s revised hostile bid of $70 per share, or $8.3 billion, saying the price did not reflect ITT's inherent value.

Instead, the New York-based owner of Sheraton hotels and Caesars casinos said it will pursue its strategy of splitting into three separate companies, buying back 26 percent of its stock for $70 a share and restructuring debt. That move, announced in July, has been challenged in federal court by Hilton.

In a statement, ITT said its board of directors voted unanimously to recommend that shareholders turn down Beverly Hills, Calif.-based Hilton's offer. The board's move had been widely expected after Hilton last week boosted the original offer of $55 per share, or $6.5 billion, made in January.

"Our board of directors has conducted a thorough review of Hilton's revised offer and has unanimously concluded that the prompt execution of ITT's comprehensive plan is in the best interests of our shareholders and other constitutents," said ITT Chairman Rand Araskog.

ITT believes a merger of the company could cannibalize operations of hotels and casinos that are located in the same markets as Hilton's. It also cited uncertainty about the value of Hilton's shares when exchanged for ITT shares, plus opinions of financial advisors that the revised offer is inadequate as reasons for its rejection.

Hilton claims ITT management, by splitting the company into three parts without shareholder approval is denying shareholders of a right to vote in the matter. Shareholder approval, however, is not required.
Hilton also argues a merged company could cut as much as $100 million in operating costs.

"There are no surprises here," Marc Grossman, Hilton's senior vice president of corporate affairs, said about ITT's rejection. "There was never any attempt to have the shareholders have one word of say in this."

Hilton's next move is in U.S. District Court in Nevada, where it has asked the court to block ITT from implementing its plan until a shareholder vote can be taken. But Hilton has lost previous court battles in the matter.
A hearing date has not been set. ITT looks to complete its break-up in the fall.
Hilton Chief Executive Officer Stephen Bollenbach has previously said he would not raise his $70 per share bid, and would not likely pursue ITT if it successfully implements its break-up strategy.
ITT's stock edged up 19 cents to close at $64, while Hilton rose 6 cents to $30.19, both on the New York Stock Exchange. ITT.N HLT.N
